Marathon Petroleum's stock has fallen 0.1% today and 10.7% over the past two weeks, coinciding with a sharp collapse in crude oil prices. Brent crude dropped below $90 a barrel on November 10th—the lowest since August—after President Trump signaled that the Iran conflict would end "fairly soon," easing concerns about supply disruptions. For a refiner, lower crude prices are a double-edged sword: while it cuts their input costs, it also squeezes the profit margin they earn by turning oil into gasoline and diesel (the difference between what they buy crude for and what they sell refined products for). The recent steep decline suggests that margin compression has outweighed the benefit of cheaper feedstock.

The broader headwind is a shift in political momentum away from fossil fuels. Midterm election results showed voters rejected Trump and the GOP, bringing renewable energy advocates back into power and signaling reduced support for fossil fuel interests in Congress. Combined with lingering uncertainty over whether Iran peace talks will actually materialize—Secretary of State Rubio said negotiations remain "unproductive"—the market is caught between hope for lower oil prices and worry about long-term demand for refining capacity.
